title: Function and Class Templates
objectives: Explain how function and class templates generate typed code at compile time and when instantiation actually happens
Write function templates with correct template argument deduction, including explicit template arguments
Write class templates with type and non-type parameters and predict sizeof of an instantiation
Use full specialisation and C++17 class template argument deduction (CTAD) appropriately
motivation: A PnL engine needs the same accumulate-and-report loop for double P&L, for integer lot counts, and for a fixed-point price type. Copy-pasting the loop three times is how divergence bugs start: fix one copy, forget the other two. C++ templates make the *type itself* a parameter, and the compiler stamps out a typed copy for every type you use - std::vector, std::map and every STL algorithm you already rely on are themselves templates.

blocks.md: Templates solve the oldest problem in typed languages: writing one algorithm that works for many types without paying for it at runtime. The alternatives all leak. Copy-paste diverges. `void*` throws type safety away. Virtual dispatch costs an indirect call per element. A template makes the type a parameter: you write the algorithm once, and the compiler stamps out a typed copy - an **instantiation** - for each type actually used. There is no function pointer, no boxing, no vtable: the generated machine code is what you would have handwritten. That guarantee is why templates are called a **zero-overhead abstraction**.

A function template declares `T` as a type parameter and uses it like an ordinary type. At each call site the compiler performs **template argument deduction** from the arguments. Deduction is all-or-nothing per parameter: in `midpoint(99, 100.5)` the compiler would have to make `T` both `int` and `double`, so it refuses and reports conflicting deduction. Either cast one argument or state the template argument explicitly: `midpoint<double>(99, 100.5)` computes $99 + (100.5 - 99)/2 = 99.75$.

blocks.caption: One source, one generated function per argument type.

blocks.title: What the compiler actually does
blocks.md: Nothing is generated when a template is merely parsed. Machine code for `midpoint<double>` appears only when a call instantiates it, and a template that is never used generates no code at all. This is also why template code lives in headers: the compiler must see the full definition at the point of instantiation.

Classes take two kinds of template parameters: types (`typename T`) and compile-time constants (`std::size_t N`) - the latter are **non-type template parameters**. Every distinct $(T, N)$ combination is a different, unrelated class: `FixedVec<double, 4>` and `FixedVec<double, 8>` share no code, and their `sizeof` differs. Because `N` is known at compile time the elements live inline in the object - no heap allocation, exactly like `std::array`.

blocks.caption: Each (T, N) pair instantiates its own class with its own layout.
FixedVec<double, 4> occupies 40 bytes: four doubles inline plus an 8-byte count. Every (T, N) instantiation lays out differently - and none of them carries a hidden pointer or vtable.

blocks.text: Where the code lives, and what it costs

blocks.md: The compiler needs the full template definition visible wherever an instantiation happens, so templates almost always live in headers, definitions and all. Splitting a template across a .cpp compiles cleanly but fails at link time with an *undefined reference*, because the using translation unit could not instantiate what it could not see. The flip side of generating typed copies is **code bloat**: fifty instantiations of a large algorithm mean fifty copies in the binary. Measure before worrying - small template functions usually inline to nothing - but when bloat is real, deduce toward one common type or move the type-independent core into a non-template function.

When one exact argument set deserves a different implementation, write a **full specialisation**: `template<> class FixedVec<bool, 64>` with a bit-packed body. The compiler prefers the most specialised match, silently, at compile time. A **partial specialisation** replaces a whole family instead, e.g. `template<typename T, std::size_t N> class FixedVec<T*, N>` for every pointer element type. This is how `std::vector<bool>` famously packs its bits - a compile-time decision with zero runtime cost.

Since C++17 you can often omit the template arguments of a class template altogether: **class template argument deduction** (CTAD) infers them from constructor arguments, so `std::pair px(1, 2.5)` means `std::pair<int, double>` with no `make_pair`. Your own class templates can opt in with deduction guides; the standard library already is.

blocks.caption: C++17: the compiler deduces class template arguments like it deduces function template arguments.

blocks.title: Why desks care
blocks.md: A pricing kernel written as a template instantiates once per price representation - `double`, fixed-point, decimal. The compiler inlines the right arithmetic into the hot loop, so the abstraction costs nothing at runtime; the bill arrives instead as compile time and binary size, which is usually the right trade.

guidedExercise.prompt: Write a function template `total(const std::vector<T>& v)` that returns the sum of the elements. Then trace exactly what the compiler does for two calls: `total(std::vector<double>{10.5, 11.25, 9.75, 10.0})` and `total(std::vector<int>{200, 300, -50})`. State what `T` is deduced as in each case, the returned value, and how many functions are generated.
hints: Declare `template<typename T> T total(const std::vector<T>& v)` - deduction reads the vector's element type.
Initialise the accumulator with `T sum{};` so it becomes zero of the right type for any T.
One instantiation is generated per distinct T that appears at a call site.

independentExercise.prompt: Extend the lesson's `FixedVec<T, N>` (with `push` and `total`) into a tiny fill accumulator. Instantiate `FixedVec<double, 3>`, push the fill prices 10.5, 11.25 and 9.75, and print the total. Answer precisely: (a) What is the exact type name the compiler generates? (b) What does `total()` return? (c) What is `sizeof(FixedVec<double, 3>)` on x86-64? (d) What happens inside the binary the moment someone else also creates a `FixedVec<int, 3>`?
hints: For double with no padding needs: sizeof = $N \times 8$ bytes of data plus 8 bytes for the std::size_t count.
Two instantiations from the same template are unrelated types; each generates its own push/total machine code.
independentExercise.solution:
(a) The compiler generates the concrete class `FixedVec<double, 3>` from the template - a real type in the binary, distinct from every other `FixedVec<T, N>`.

(b) $10.5 + 11.25 + 9.75 = 31.5$.

(c) $3 \times 8 = 24$ bytes of inline doubles plus the 8-byte `std::size_t` count $= \mathbf{32}$ bytes, with no padding needed (alignment 8 is satisfied).

(d) A **second, independent instantiation** `FixedVec<int, 3>` is generated: its own `push`/`total` code and layout (integers take 4 bytes, so its layout and arithmetic differ). That is code bloat's price - paid in binary size, never in per-element runtime dispatch.

commonMistakes: Defining a template only in a .cpp file - instantiation needs the full definition at the point of use, so templates live in headers and the mistake surfaces as linker errors, not compiler errors.
Calling `f(1, 2.5)` against a single-type-parameter template: T is deduced as both int and double and deduction fails. Cast an argument or write `f<double>(1, 2.5)`.
Writing `T sum = 0;` instead of `T sum{};` - the first fails to compile for types with no constructor from int.
Assuming the compiler checks all template code at definition: dependent code is diagnosed only at instantiation, so bugs can stay hidden until a new type is used.
Forgetting that every distinct (T, N) set generates another copy of the code - instantiating a big template across dozens of types bloats the binary.
realWorldApplication: The entire STL is templates, and low-latency pricing engines use templates to specialise hot kernels per instrument or price representation at compile time, deliberately trading binary size and compile time for zero runtime dispatch.
quantFinanceApplication: An order book template instantiates once per price/quantity type - double for research, fixed-point for production - and the compiler weaves the correct arithmetic into the hot path with no virtual calls on any tick.
summary: Templates parameterise code on types (`typename T`) and compile-time values (`std::size_t N`); the compiler instantiates a typed copy at each point of use.
An unused template generates no code; each distinct argument set costs binary size, never per-element runtime dispatch.
Deduction is per-parameter and all-or-nothing: `f(1, 2.5)` fails with one T - cast, or specify `f<double>(1, 2.5)`.
Full specialisations (`template<>`) and partial specialisations replace the primary template for specific argument sets; the most specialised match wins.
Since C++17, CTAD deduces class template arguments from constructor calls: `std::pair px(1, 2.5)`.

quiz.prompt: When does the compiler actually generate machine code for `midpoint<double>`?
options: As soon as it parses the template definition
When it reaches a call such as `midpoint(99.0, 101.0)` and instantiates T = double
At program startup, once for every type it can imagine
At link time, when the linker resolves the call
quiz.explanation: Instantiation happens at the point of use with concrete template arguments. Parsing a template generates nothing, and an unused template generates no code at all.

quiz.prompt: What does this C++17 program print?
quiz.explanation: `twice(21)` instantiates `twice<int>`: 42. `twice(1.5)` instantiates `twice<double>`: 3.0, printed by iostream as `3`. The explicit `twice<double>(21)` forces T = double even for the int literal: 21.0 + 21.0 = 42.0, printed as `42`.

quiz.prompt: Given `template<typename T> struct Box { T v; };`, what is `sizeof(Box<double>)` on x86-64?
quiz.explanation: The struct contains exactly one 8-byte double. A template adds no hidden members - no tag, no pointer - so the wrapper's size equals its member's size.

quiz.prompt: You define a class template entirely in one .cpp file and use it from another translation unit. What happens?
options: It works: templates are automatically exported like inline functions
The compiler silently duplicates the definition into every translation unit
A linker error: the using translation unit cannot instantiate a template whose full definition it never saw
quiz.explanation: The compiler needs the full template definition visible at the point of instantiation. A .cpp-only definition compiles but produces an *undefined reference* at link time - the classic reason templates live in headers.

quiz.prompt: A primary template `FixedVec<T, N>` exists, plus `template<> class FixedVec<bool, 64>`. What code does `FixedVec<bool, 64> x;` use?
options: A compile error: exact-argument specialisations are not allowed
The specialised version - a full specialisation wins over the primary template
The primary template with sizeof(bool) rounded up
quiz.explanation: A full specialisation replaces the primary template for that exact argument set. This is the mechanism behind `std::vector<bool>`'s bit packing.

quiz.prompt: What does this C++17 program print?
quiz.explanation: `Fixed<double, 4>` holds four 8-byte doubles = 32 bytes; `Fixed<char, 10>` holds ten 1-byte chars = 10 bytes. The template adds no hidden members; each (T, N) instantiation is exactly its data.

flashcards.back: The concrete function or class the compiler generates from a template for one specific set of template arguments (e.g. midpoint<double>). Each distinct argument set generates separate code; unused templates generate none.

flashcards.front: template<typename T, int N> struct Fixed { T data[N]; }; What is sizeof(Fixed<double, 4>) on x86-64?
flashcards.back: 32 - four 8-byte doubles. Templates add no hidden members or tags.

flashcards.front: Why must template definitions live in headers?
flashcards.back: The compiler needs the full definition visible at the point of instantiation. A .cpp-only definition gives undefined-reference linker errors from other translation units.
Full: one exact argument set is replaced, template<> class X<bool, 64>. Partial: a whole family is replaced, template<typename T> class X<T*, N>. The most specialised match wins.
